en: [1] Om, homage to the Buddha!

He who is glorious and of pure intellect, a thunderbolt to the mountain of others' misconceptions, a leader among those who possess valid authority by virtue of his flourishing manliness in composing excellent treatises;
... ... ... ... ... this secret is composed by me for the delight of those of feeble intellect, in accordance with the nature of reality (dharmatā).
When one investigates the secrets of logic, the scriptural statements become a refuge for doubt.

Since the attainment of what is beneficial and the avoidance of what is harmful must necessarily be preceded by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), this treatise is commenced for the purpose of instructing those who do not understand it.
... ... ... Objects [of knowledge] are established through their negation by means of valid cognition.
Valid cognition is non-contradictory knowledge; it is the stability of causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*).
[2] *Sambā-mū-pā*:
Furthermore, that which is non-concordant (*visaṃvādin*) is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

By the word "means of valid cognition," which is established through its instrumentality (*karaṇa*), agency (*kartṛtva*) is preceded by the implication of the action upon the object; it is the most effective means (*sādhakatama*)... [that which is] predominant.
The collection of body and sense-faculties that accompanies that [cognition] is called its "most efficient instrument" (*sādhakatama*).

Furthermore, action (*karman*) is purposeful activity (*arthakriyā*), which is also the result of valid cognition (*pramiti*). According to the principle, "How can those things that are mostly devoid of designation come into being?", it is the capacity to bring about what is capable of purposeful activity regarding the object of engagement (*pravṛttiviṣaya-niyama*).
However, it is not merely the attainment of the object; for that [attainment] is... [correspondence] ...the root... the path... [variant readings].
Because it would be useless for those practical agents who desire to attain an object not yet demonstrated through activity;
for what [purpose] would they have if the object were already cognized by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)?
If that cognition of theirs is an auxiliary factor for activity and attainment toward that desired object, [then it serves a purpose].

If that is so—[4] just as it is useful for them, in that very same way... [omission] ...in that very same way, then it is useful for those conventional users even when it is not functioning; and mere investigation (*paryeṣaṇāmātra*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Even in the case of a definitive determination (*pariccheda*), it serves solely as a factor for the attainment of engagement; moreover,
this has not been explained in that manner in other philosophical systems.
And it has been explained by the Master in this way: "[It is] non-discrepant" (*avisaṃvādī*).
"Object" (*artha*) refers to burning and so forth, because it is that which is to be sought (*eṣaṇīyatva*).
The stability of that accomplishment of action which resides in the karma is its immovability;
this is for the purpose of excluding sleep.
[6] *sambā-mū-pā*.

For one who has awakened in the morning from a dream, there is an immediate appearance that is not faded. In this context, the word *avisamvādi* (non-contradictory) is formed by adding a possessive suffix (*matvarthīya*) to the term *sa*—which here appears as *ta* without the visarga—as it is joined with the word *parisamvādī*. Thus, the term *avisamvādi* is well-established in relation to a person’s engagement in what is to be abandoned or their avoidance of what is to be adopted, specifically regarding purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) and its means.
The opinion of the Bhāṣya; [8] samvā-mū-pā;
[9] samvā-mū-pā.
[10] That which is without the *visarga* is *pā-mū-pu*.
However, according to the view of Dharmottara:

"In a case where the term 'non-discrepant' (*avisamvādi*) is absent, it is well-known that [the word] brings about the attainment of the object as its form is presented; for example, users of language say, 'This person is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because he is non-discrepant. [11–12] They say this regarding those who bring about the attainment of an object whose form has been displayed.
[11] *saṃvā-mū-pā* / [12] *saṃvā-mū-pā* / Even though—

The quality of being a means of valid cognition (*prāpakatva*) was already obtained from the word *pramāṇa*; it was merely made explicit by the inclusion of the term "non-discrepant" (*avisamvādin*), since that term is primarily used as a designation. Even where the word "non-discrepant" does not occur, it is understood to be included by the term "non-discrepant" in the Vārttika—[where the reading is *samvāda*].
[14] The purpose of the statement regarding the origin of the term "means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*) is to explain the grounds for its application.

According to the view of the Bhāṣya, however, the term "non-discrepant" (*avisaṃvādi*) indicates that the definition pertains to worldly objects (*laukikārthatva*). [Note: *samvā-* is a variant reading for *visaṃvā-*; *mū-pā* refers to the root text and commentary.]
For everyone who seeks purposeful action— whether it be valid or invalid cognition— investigates [it], not out of mere habit or whim. Indeed, a discerning person does not act out of addiction.
Valid cognition is not merely the apprehension of an object;
what then?
That which has been stated by others is indeed distinguished;
and for that [cognition], the sense organs and so forth are not the most effective means of accomplishment (*sādhakatama*), according to the reasoning to be stated later.
What then?
The conformity with the object resides in the cognition;
therefore, because it consists of that [conformity], cognition alone is the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa),
not the sense organs and so forth.

Perception and inference— the cognition of the first moment— by determining through the restriction of its specific form that an object is capable of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) as excluded from what is not of that nature, and by virtue of the ascertainment of the agent who performs its own operation produced by its own power, becomes the cause of its own occurrence and touches upon the status of being a means for attaining [the goal].
For its capacity to incite activity is nothing other than this very operation of indicating [the object].
Furthermore, there is no "causing-to-attain" other than "setting-in-motion," for knowledge does not set one in motion by taking him by the hand;
nor does inference, like a blind man following another person, cause the person to attain the object by following the person's location. Rather—

It is precisely by demonstrating its capacity for purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) that [cognition] prompts activity; it prompts activity by pointing out the object that is the domain of engagement and brings it about.
And this is the sole function of all cognitions, namely, the presentation of the object.
Therefore, that other [cognition], because it apprehends an object already apprehended, is not a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*).
But is it not the case that—
since there is no further function such as instigation (*pravartakatva*) beyond the presentation of the object— [the first cognition alone suffices]?
In that case, would this not result in a redundancy?
[The term *pravṛtti*] would be shown as "it causes to proceed," "it sets in motion," "it displays the object of activity," and "it brings about [attainment]."
Since this is the meaning of the sentence, it is not correct for the opponent to have considered that "it might show" or "it shows";

for what is called "activity" (pravṛtti)— which has the definition to be stated later— is indeed non-different from "showing," and its attainment elsewhere consists precisely in the form of touching with the hand and so forth.
Furthermore,
it is said that this much alone constitutes the basis for the occurrence and attainment of that [result], namely the manifestation of knowledge itself,
and not through any other operation.

[18] For example—when there are many potential killers, such as the gatekeeper, the executioner, and the lord of the earth, and because someone is of some utility [to the king], it is said that the king’s status as a killer consists solely in his issuing the command; when this is stated, do they say, "commanding, commanding"? [19–20] Indeed, they do.
Having written "go-mū-pā" [19] and "māvajñā" [20], the "mū-pu" was as if severed;
for what indeed is called death but the very breaking apart of one who is bound?
Because it serves as the cause for that [bondage], the act of issuing a command (*ājñādāna*) fulfills its purpose by excluding other operations; thus, it is indeed something distinct.
This should be understood in the same way here as well.
To the question: "When there are many means of attainment (*prāpaka*), such as mere knowledge, objects, and so forth, how does knowledge bring about attainment?"—[the answer follows].
The reply is: "There is no tautology in the phrase 'showing [it] indeed'.
Now, one might object: this very thing has been stated in many places—
"Unfit for the attainment of that which is capable of purposeful action"—
how is this to be determined?
Does it mean that the accomplishment of the action of burning or the like, which is the object to be acquired, is possible therein?
If it were so [that the definition applies to all objects],
there would be the deficiency of not including that which is capable of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) as something to be abandoned (*heya*).
Furthermore, the validity (*prāmāṇya*) of a cognition whose object is such purposeful action would not be encompassed.
[21] Here, having written "ma," it is as if the root were severed.

For one who asserts that "valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is a cognition capable of leading to the attainment of an object-sufficient for the intended purposeful action (*arthakriyā*)"— even that which leads to the attainment of purposeful action does not constitute the very essence of valid cognition here.

Now, that which is sought after (*arthyate*) is called an "object" (*artha*); that which is sought for the purpose of abandoning or acquiring, such as burning and so forth, is precisely what is meant here.

Having written *atra ti*, it appears as if the beginning of the word was torn away; the intended meaning is a *virūpaikaśeṣa* (an elliptical compound consisting of dissimilar members) expressing both "purposeful action" (*arthakriyā*) and "that which is capable of purposeful action" (*arthakriyāsamartha*).
[23] And how is it that— "valid cognition is that which is capable of bringing about attainment"?
If this is said, would that which directly brings about purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) be included?
True;
this very point is what is held in mind.
The phrase "capable of causal efficiency" (*arthakriyāsamartha*) was stated as an illustration;
by this, it should be understood that even that which does not bring about causal efficiency is fit to be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

In the definition of conceptualization as "a cognition whose appearance is capable of being associated with verbal expression," just as the word "capable" includes that which is actually associated with verbal expression as well as that which is not, yet is fully developed and suitable for such association,
so too should it be established here.
That which is fit for attainment and that which is the direct attainer—
both of these must be encompassed by the term "fit" (yogya). Furthermore,

since self-cognizing perception possesses an excellence in its status as an attainer with respect to its own object of cognition (meya), it should be understood that the general definition [of valid cognition] remains intact in this case as well.
[24] Memory (*smṛti*),
inference (*anumāna*), and perception (*pratyakṣa*)— its conformity with the object is also easily established given its identity [with that object].
If the preceding [cognition] possesses the status of a means of valid cognition (*mānatā*) because it is the cause for the attainment of the subsequent [cognition],...
In that very same way, since the latter is equally appropriate, why is it not [the case]?
Therefore,
let it be understood that the validity of all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is intrinsic (*svataḥ*);
for a capacity (*śakti*) that does not exist intrinsically cannot be produced by anything else.
[25] For that which does not exist inherently... cannot be established—Ta-saṃ-paṃ 745, 813 pṛ. / [26] If all means of valid cognition were to be apprehended inherently... it could not be established.
The first half [of the verse] is at Ta-saṃ-paṃ 745, pṛ. 2812, kā; the second half is in the commentary on that same [verse] at 2811.
For there are four positions:
(1) that both validity and invalidity are intrinsic;
or (2) that invalidity is intrinsic while validity is extrinsic.
Or rather, is this validity or invalidity extrinsic (*parataḥ*) or intrinsic (*svataḥ*)?
Nevertheless, validity is extrinsic (*parataḥ*). In that regard—
The first [position] is not tenable because it entails two mutually contradictory consequences;
the second is not tenable because the negation of validity through non-apprehension is possible;
and although invalidity might [occur] through its own non-apprehension, [the following applies].
Nevertheless, even validity depends on external factors such as corroboration, the cognition of excellence, and the purpose;
[corroboration—Mūla, Pāṭha]. [Corroboration—Mūla, Pāṭha].
Then—
why is the cognition of the quality of correspondence not considered superior? (31) [The variants *samvāda*, *mūla*, and *pā* appear in the commentary.]
If there were dependence [on other factors], validity would never be established anywhere.
[However, it is] held that in some cases, [validity is established] through the cognition of correspondence and excellence.
[The first half only] ta-saṃ-paṃ 787 pṛ.
[33] Regarding dependence, the status of being a means of valid cognition... in some cases.
Therefore, according to the principle that "the third [alternative] is not [possible]," the third [option] is not [tenable].
Consequently—
By the consequence of intrinsic validity (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*), the presence of subverting causes and defects is established; for,
according to the principle that "it is due to the two cognitions being unfit for that," validity is intrinsic.
The argument that "invalidity arises from another source" is thereby refuted as being logical;
for validity is indeed dependent [on other factors].

Indeed, non-contradiction (*avisaṃvāditva*) arises through a causal connection with the cognition of the state and its cause, whereas in the case of that which directly causes attainment, it exists through identity (*tādātmya*).
[35] Because it is established by means of coexistence (sahabhū), non-obstruction (apratighāta), and the capacity for action (kāritra), validity (prāmāṇya) indeed remains fixed;
therefore—
"By means of confirmation alone, confirmation must again be sought in that very same way..."— thus is the infinite regress (anavasthā) rejected.

as for the second [alternative]:

the cognition of that is "verbal" (*śābda*).

it is to be connected with the context as "the stability of purposeful action" (*arthakriyāsthitir*), which is non-discrepancy (*avisaṃvādanam*).

That cognition, even if it concerns a previously unknown object, is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because it is useless for those engaged in practical activity (*vyavahartṛ*). According to this principle:
having taken as the basis the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) which is capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsamartha*), even though the universal (*sāmānya*) is incapable—

Since the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) is capable [of its function] by virtue of being an object to be determined (*adhyavaseya*), the cognition that does not have that [characteristic itself] as its object is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
And that [object] is necessarily demonstrated, capable of being attained, and existent.

knowledge, whether arising sequentially or arising in successive succession, is observed to have the capacity to manifest a specifically determined object.

Or rather, when one proceeds without seeing any restrictive factor through any sign or conceptual construction, an object that is indeterminate with respect to existence and non-existence must be shown;
and what is indeterminate cannot be attained.
And although it is indeed shown by erroneous cognition (*viparyāsajñāna*),
nevertheless, because it is not shown as being existent, it cannot be attained.
In that regard—
Some error is non-conceptual,
such as the cognition of the duality of the Lord of the Night;
some consists of conceptualization.

For example: when there is a conflict regarding a mass of mirage-rays in the desert, there is the superimposition of water. For that [superimposition], arising by depending on the restrictive factor—the necessarily appearing mirage-ray—is of the nature of a logical doubt.
What then?
It is indeed a misconception;
for, regarding an object that is appearing, the conceptualization or ascertainment produced by the force of that appearance must be either [correct] or a misconception.
Doubt, however,
is a conceptual construction (vikalpa) that takes two simultaneously appearing forms as its object;
but regarding an imperceptible object, doubt is a conceptual construction in which two forms appear together and are logically connected.
Just as the conceptual construction (vikalpa) that "my protector will come tomorrow" is a logical doubt, so too is that which arises from the Veda.
By this—
[it is shown that] invalidity is divided into three kinds by way of falsity, ignorance, and doubt.

If the operation characterized by avoidance arises from the desire to avoid, then knowledge, while being employed as that which causes avoidance, must be called a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) only insofar as it causes attainment.

because that [cognition] is endowed with the capacity to lead [to the object], which is based on the non-deviation from the snake, the poison, and the thorn;
therefore—
It has become something to be avoided; otherwise, it would be a root defeat.

the doubt conforms to the form that does not appear [as real],
